title: The hunter and the birds
hookLine: Valmiki sees a hunter kill one of two birds, and his grief becomes the first verse

cards: A sage named Valmiki walks down to the Tamasa river to bathe. In a tree nearby, two krauncha birds, a pair, are calling to each other. A hunter's arrow strikes one, and it falls to the ground.
Its mate circles it, crying. Valmiki is so moved that words burst out of him: hunter, may you find no rest for endless years, for you killed one of a pair lost in love. Then he stops, startled.
The words came out in a perfect meter. The Ramayana says his grief, shoka, became verse, shloka. The first poem.

teach.b: The Ramayana tells this as the moment its own poetry began: with a man who couldn't bear harm done to a bird. That's the first limb of yoga in a story.
Sutra 2.30 names the five yamas, the restraints. Ahimsa, non-harm. Satya, truthfulness.

Asteya, not stealing. Brahmacharya, restraint, which the classical commentary reads as sexual restraint and many householder teachers read as faithfulness and moderation. And aparigraha, not grasping.
The commentary traditionally credited to Vyasa makes the key move: ahimsa is the root, and the other four are there to serve it.
Even truth serves non-harm: speech should be for the good of all beings, and a true sentence spoken to wound only looks like virtue. Sutra 2.31 raises the stakes.
These five become the great vow, mahavrata, when they hold everywhere, with no exceptions for kind of being, place, time or occasion.
The commentary's example of a limited vow sounds like Valmiki's river: a fisherman who says, I'll harm only fish.

teach.h: THE GREAT VOW HAS NO FINE PRINT.
teach.b: The great vow has no fine print. The bird counts too. You'll see this root at Hindu tables.

Many Hindus, though not all, eat vegetarian food because of ahimsa, and many who eat meat keep it off the plate on holy days. The word traveled far: Jains and Buddhists hold it dear, and Gandhi carried it into politics.
In the sutras it's quieter. It's page one.

how: In classical yoga teaching the five yamas come before any posture or breathing practice; in Hindu homes ahimsa is a common reason families eat vegetarian food, especially on holy days, and renunciants may take the yamas as formal vows.

o: five daily prayers said at sunrise

games.q: the five yamas — tap the pairs.

s: the Ramayana tradition says the first verse came from grief over a bird
Valmiki's grief, shoka, became verse, shloka.
the commentary says the other yamas are there for the sake of non-harm
ahimsa is the root; the others make it purer.
a vow with exceptions for place or time is the great vow
2.31: the great vow applies everywhere, with no exceptions of kind, place, time or occasion.

games.q: a fisherman says, I'll practice non-harm, except toward fish. what does sutra 2.31 call his vow?
o: a limited vow, not yet the great one.
games.why: the commentary uses exactly this fisherman: his non-harm is limited by kind of being. the great vow, mahavrata, has no such limits.

practice: Notice the tone of the voice in your head, and whether a thought arrives with a little harshness, toward yourself or someone else.
Don't argue with it; just soften the tone, the way you'd lower your voice near a sleeping child, and let the thought go on its way. Then rest with the breath until the next one.

wordCard.voice: Yama. The restraints, the first limb of yoga: non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint and non-grasping.

orig.note: Sanskrit ahiṃsā: a (not) plus hiṃsā (harm, injury); the first of the yamas.

carryVoice: Your line: ahimsa, non-harm, is the root. Valmiki's grief for one bird began the Ramayana. Until tomorrow.
